system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Paroxysmal facial pain arises in the distribution of the trigeminal nerve, often from focal nerve-root irritation or compression.
vignette: A 62-year-old woman has recurrent episodes of severe electric-shock pain over the right cheek and upper lip. Each attack lasts seconds and is triggered by brushing her teeth or touching the face. Neurologic examination between attacks is normal.
distractor_notes: Cluster headache lasts much longer and is accompanied by ipsilateral autonomic symptoms.
Migraine typically lasts hours and is not triggered by light tactile stimulation of a trigeminal distribution.
Postherpetic neuralgia follows a prior zoster eruption and causes persistent neuropathic pain rather than brief triggerable attacks.
TMJ pain is mechanical and localized near the joint rather than lancinating trigeminal-distribution shocks.
key_expl: Brief, unilateral, triggerable electric-shock facial pain in a trigeminal distribution is classic for trigeminal neuralgia.
objective: Recognize trigeminal neuralgia from paroxysmal triggerable unilateral facial pain.

sources.title: Trigeminal neuralgia
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes brief, severe, shock-like facial pain in trigeminal distributions that can be triggered by routine facial stimulation.

sources.title: Trigeminal Neuralgia
sources.support: NINDS describes recurrent severe facial pain along trigeminal branches and common trigger phenomena.

system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Loss of SMN protein from biallelic SMN1 dysfunction causes degeneration of anterior horn lower motor neurons, producing symmetric proximal weakness and hypotonia with preserved sensation.
vignette: A 5-month-old infant has poor head control, symmetric proximal weakness, hypotonia, tongue fasciculations, and absent deep tendon reflexes. Sensation appears intact.
lead: Which cellular population is primarily affected?
distractor_notes: Sensory neurons are not the principal target and sensation is generally preserved.
Upper motor neuron injury would cause hyperreflexia and spasticity rather than areflexic hypotonia.
Purkinje-cell disease causes ataxia rather than a pure lower motor neuron syndrome.
Postsynaptic receptor disease causes fatigable weakness without motor neuron degeneration or tongue fasciculations.
key_expl: SMA is a lower motor neuron disease caused by SMN1 dysfunction, with degeneration of anterior horn cells.
objective: Link infantile hypotonia, areflexia, and fasciculations to anterior horn cell degeneration in SMA.

sources.title: Spinal muscular atrophy
sources.support: MedlinePlus Genetics describes SMN1-related motor neuron loss causing weakness and muscle atrophy.

sources.title: Spinal Muscular Atrophy
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes SMA as a genetic disease affecting motor neurons and causing progressive weakness.

system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Tourette syndrome is defined clinically by multiple motor tics plus at least one vocal tic beginning before age 18 and persisting for at least 1 year.
vignette: A 12-year-old boy has had repeated eye blinking, shoulder shrugging, and throat clearing for 18 months. The movements and sounds wax and wane and are briefly suppressible.
distractor_notes: Provisional tic disorder lasts less than 1 year.
Persistent motor tic disorder involves motor or vocal tics, but not both categories as required for Tourette syndrome.
OCD involves intrusive thoughts and compulsions rather than involuntary motor and vocal tics.
Focal motor seizures are not typically suppressible and do not present as chronic waxing-and-waning motor plus vocal tics.
key_expl: Motor and vocal tics for more than 1 year with childhood onset meet the core diagnostic pattern of Tourette syndrome.
objective: Differentiate Tourette syndrome from other tic disorders using tic type and duration.

sources.title: Diagnosing Tic Disorders
sources.support: CDC states that Tourette syndrome requires both motor and vocal tics with tic symptoms for at least 1 year and onset before age 18.

sources.title: Tourette Syndrome
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes chronic motor and vocal tics beginning in childhood.

system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: OCD consists of intrusive unwanted obsessions and/or repetitive compulsions performed to reduce distress, consuming time or impairing function.
vignette: A 27-year-old woman spends 3 hours each evening repeatedly checking that her stove is off. She knows the behavior is excessive but experiences intense anxiety if she tries to resist because of intrusive fears that her apartment will burn down.
distractor_notes: GAD causes excessive worry across multiple domains without stereotyped rituals performed to neutralize intrusive obsessions.
OCPD involves ego-syntonic perfectionism and rigidity rather than ego-dystonic intrusive thoughts and compulsions.
Panic disorder causes recurrent unexpected panic attacks, not hours of ritualized checking.
Delusional disorder involves fixed false beliefs with impaired insight rather than recognized excessive compulsions.
key_expl: Ego-dystonic intrusive harm fears relieved by repetitive checking are classic obsessions and compulsions.
objective: Recognize OCD from intrusive unwanted thoughts and repetitive anxiety-reducing rituals.

sources.title: Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder: What You Need to Know
sources.support: NIMH describes obsessions as intrusive unwanted thoughts and compulsions as repetitive behaviors performed in response.

sources.title: Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes recurrent obsessions and compulsions that interfere with daily life.

system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Panic disorder features recurrent unexpected panic attacks plus persistent concern or maladaptive behavior related to future attacks.
vignette: A 31-year-old man has had four abrupt episodes of intense fear with palpitations, dyspnea, chest tightness, trembling, and fear of dying. The attacks peak within minutes and occur unexpectedly. For 2 months he has avoided exercise because he fears another attack.
distractor_notes: GAD is chronic diffuse worry rather than recurrent discrete unexpected attacks peaking within minutes.
PTSD requires a traumatic exposure syndrome with re-experiencing, avoidance, negative mood/cognition, and hyperarousal.
Social anxiety is tied to social scrutiny or performance situations rather than unexpected attacks.
Hyperthyroidism can cause palpitations and anxiety but does not by itself explain recurrent stereotyped unexpected panic attacks with anticipatory avoidance.
key_expl: Recurrent unexpected panic attacks followed by persistent concern and avoidance establish the clinical pattern of panic disorder.
objective: Recognize panic disorder from unexpected panic attacks plus persistent concern or behavioral change.

sources.title: Panic Disorder: What You Need to Know
sources.support: NIMH describes recurrent unexpected panic attacks and persistent worry or behavioral changes related to future attacks.

sources.title: Panic Disorder Statistics
sources.support: NIMH defines panic disorder by recurrent unexpected panic attacks with persistent concern or behavioral change.

system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: PTSD develops after traumatic exposure and includes intrusive re-experiencing, avoidance, negative alterations in cognition/mood, and hyperarousal lasting more than 1 month.
vignette: A combat veteran has nightmares and intrusive memories of an explosion 8 months ago, avoids crowded places that remind him of the event, feels emotionally detached, and startles easily.
distractor_notes: Acute stress disorder is limited to the first month after trauma.
Adjustment disorder does not require the characteristic intrusion, avoidance, and hyperarousal clusters after severe trauma.
GAD is broad chronic worry and does not require a traumatic trigger with re-experiencing.
Major depression can cause detachment and sleep change but does not by itself explain trauma-specific nightmares, avoidance, and hypervigilance.
key_expl: Persistent trauma-related intrusion, avoidance, detachment, and hyperarousal for 8 months are characteristic of PTSD.
objective: Recognize PTSD from its trauma-linked symptom clusters and duration.

sources.title: Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder
sources.support: NIMH describes PTSD after trauma with intrusive symptoms, avoidance, cognition/mood changes, and arousal/reactivity symptoms.

sources.title: Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder Statistics
sources.support: NIMH provides the diagnostic framing and epidemiology of PTSD.

system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Degeneration of the macula impairs sharp central vision while peripheral vision is relatively preserved; neovascular AMD involves abnormal vessels that damage the macula.
vignette: A 74-year-old woman reports progressive difficulty reading and recognizing faces. Straight lines appear wavy. Peripheral vision is preserved.
lead: Which retinal region is primarily responsible for the lost visual function?
distractor_notes: The optic disc carries exiting axons and has no photoreceptors; it is not the center of sharp straight-ahead vision.
Peripheral retina supports peripheral visual fields rather than high-acuity central vision.
The ciliary body produces aqueous humor and participates in accommodation.
The iris regulates pupil size and light entry.
key_expl: AMD damages the macula, the retinal region responsible for detailed straight-ahead central vision.
objective: Link central visual distortion in older adults to macular pathology.
clues: older adult with central vision loss

sources.title: Age-Related Macular Degeneration
sources.support: NEI explains that AMD damages the macula and causes blurry or wavy central vision.

sources.title: Eye Conditions and Diseases
sources.support: NEI identifies AMD among retinal disorders affecting vision.

system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Lens proteins aggregate and the lens becomes cloudy, scattering/blocking light and producing progressive painless blurry vision, glare, faded colors, and poor night vision.
vignette: A 78-year-old man has slowly progressive painless blurry vision, glare from headlights, halos around lights, and faded colors. Funduscopic view is obscured by lens opacity.
distractor_notes: Corneal disease can blur vision but would not be described as a cloudy lens opacity.
Macular disease primarily impairs central retinal vision rather than causing an opaque lens and glare.
Optic neuropathy causes afferent visual dysfunction rather than a visible lens opacity.
Trabecular meshwork dysfunction is central to open-angle glaucoma, not cataract formation.
key_expl: A cataract is clouding of the lens due largely to age-related changes and aggregation of lens proteins.
objective: Identify the lens as the site of pathology in age-related cataract.

sources.title: Cataracts
sources.support: NEI defines cataract as a cloudy area in the lens and describes blurry vision, faded colors, glare, and poor night vision.

sources.title: Causes of Cataracts
sources.support: NEI explains that lens proteins break down and clump, making the lens cloudy.

system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Acute occlusion of the central retinal artery abruptly stops retinal perfusion and causes sudden painless monocular vision loss.
vignette: A 72-year-old man with carotid atherosclerosis suddenly loses vision in his left eye without pain. Fundus examination shows a pale retina with a cherry-red fovea.
distractor_notes: CRVO typically causes diffuse retinal hemorrhages and venous engorgement rather than a pale retina.
Retinal detachment often causes flashes, floaters, and a curtain-like field defect rather than a pale retina with cherry-red fovea.
Acute angle-closure glaucoma is painful with a red eye and elevated intraocular pressure.
Optic neuritis usually causes painful eye movement and does not produce the classic pale-retina/cherry-red-fovea pattern.
key_expl: Sudden painless monocular blindness with retinal pallor and a cherry-red fovea is classic for CRAO.
objective: Recognize central retinal artery occlusion as an ocular vascular emergency causing abrupt painless monocular vision loss.

sources.title: Central retinal artery occlusion
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes sudden painless vision loss from retinal artery blockage and common embolic sources.

sources.title: Retinal Disorders
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes retinal vascular disorders as causes of visual loss.

system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Central retinal vein obstruction impairs venous outflow, causing retinal venous congestion, hemorrhage, edema, and painless visual loss.
vignette: A 68-year-old woman with hypertension develops sudden painless blurry vision in one eye. Fundoscopy shows dilated tortuous retinal veins, optic-disc edema, and widespread retinal hemorrhages.
distractor_notes: CRAO produces retinal pallor with a cherry-red fovea rather than diffuse hemorrhagic venous congestion.
Vitreous hemorrhage may obscure the fundus but does not produce the classic diffuse retinal venous engorgement and hemorrhage pattern.
Retinal detachment causes a detached retinal contour and curtain-like field loss.
Acute angle-closure glaucoma is painful with elevated intraocular pressure and corneal haze.
key_expl: Painless monocular visual loss with diffuse retinal hemorrhages and dilated tortuous veins is characteristic of CRVO.
objective: Differentiate central retinal vein occlusion from central retinal artery occlusion by funduscopic pattern.
clues: dilated veins with diffuse retinal hemorrhages

sources.title: Central Retinal Vein Occlusion
sources.support: NEI describes CRVO as blockage of the main retinal vein causing visual symptoms from impaired retinal venous drainage.

sources.title: Retinal vein occlusion
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes retinal vein blockage with painless vision change and retinal hemorrhagic findings.

system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Expanded CAG repeats in the androgen receptor gene cause an X-linked lower motor neuron disease in adult males with bulbar/proximal weakness plus signs of androgen insensitivity such as gynecomastia and reduced fertility.
vignette: A 46-year-old man develops progressive proximal weakness, muscle cramps, tongue fasciculations, dysarthria, gynecomastia, and infertility. His maternal uncle had a similar disorder.
lead: Which molecular abnormality is most likely?
correct: CAG repeat expansion in the androgen receptor gene
distractor_notes: FMR1 CGG expansion causes fragile X syndrome rather than adult X-linked motor neuron disease with androgen-related findings.
HTT CAG expansion causes Huntington disease with chorea and neuropsychiatric/cognitive manifestations.
SMN1 loss causes spinal muscular atrophy, usually with earlier onset and no androgen-insensitivity manifestations.
FXN GAA expansion causes Friedreich ataxia with sensory/cerebellar and cardiomyopathic features.
key_expl: Kennedy disease is an X-linked CAG-repeat disorder of the androgen receptor producing lower motor neuron degeneration and androgen-insensitivity features.
objective: Link adult male lower motor neuron disease plus gynecomastia/infertility to androgen-receptor CAG expansion.
clues: gynecomastia and infertility with X-linked pedigree

sources.title: Spinal and bulbar muscular atrophy
sources.support: MedlinePlus Genetics describes androgen receptor CAG expansion, X-linked inheritance, motor neuron degeneration, gynecomastia, and infertility.

sources.title: AR gene
sources.support: MedlinePlus Genetics describes androgen receptor function and repeat-expansion variants causing spinal and bulbar muscular atrophy.

system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: GAD is excessive, difficult-to-control worry about multiple everyday domains on most days for at least 6 months, accompanied by symptoms such as restlessness, fatigue, poor concentration, irritability, muscle tension, or sleep disturbance.
vignette: A 35-year-old woman has worried excessively about work, finances, her parents' health, and household tasks almost every day for 9 months. She finds the worry difficult to control and has muscle tension, irritability, and insomnia. She has no discrete panic attacks.
distractor_notes: Panic disorder centers on recurrent unexpected panic attacks rather than persistent multi-domain worry.
OCD requires obsessions and/or compulsions, which are not present here.
Adjustment disorder is tied to a specific identifiable stressor and does not require the persistent multi-domain worry pattern of GAD.
PTSD requires exposure to trauma and characteristic intrusion, avoidance, mood/cognition, and hyperarousal symptoms.
key_expl: Excessive difficult-to-control worry across many domains for more than 6 months with tension and sleep symptoms is GAD.
objective: Recognize generalized anxiety disorder from persistent multi-domain worry and associated somatic/cognitive symptoms.

sources.title: Generalized Anxiety Disorder: What You Need to Know
sources.support: NIMH describes excessive difficult-to-control worry on most days for at least 6 months with associated symptoms.

sources.title: Generalized Anxiety Disorder Statistics
sources.support: NIMH defines GAD as excessive anxiety and worry across events or activities for at least 6 months with functional impact.
